title: Among the Quadi
hookLine: a note says book two was written in camp on the river Granua, at war

lines: A LINE AT THE END OF BOOK ONE.
cards: Where do you picture the Meditations being written? A marble study, maybe, with a view over Rome. A quiet library.
Scrolls, oil lamps, silence. Then you reach the end of book one, and there, in the manuscripts, is a short line that changes the picture. It isn't philosophy.
It's a place name. Among the Quadi, at the Granua. A tribe and a river, far from Rome, on the edge of the empire, in the middle of a war.

teach.h: AMONG THE QUADI, AT THE GRANUA.
teach.b: First, the note. Between books one and two, the manuscripts carry a few words: among the Quadi, at the Granua. The Quadi were a Germanic people living north of the Danube.
The Granua is a river there, usually identified with the Hron, which flows through what's now Slovakia. Second, the war.
The historian Cassius Dio tells of Marcus on the Danube frontier, leading campaigns against the Marcomanni, the Quadi and other peoples, year after year.
The emperor spent long seasons in army camps, in the cold, far from Rome. Third, where the note belongs. Scholars aren't agreed.

teach.h: END OF BOOK ONE, OR START OF TWO?
teach.b: It could close book one, or head book two. Some editors read it as a heading for book two, because a similar note, at Carnuntum, a legionary fortress on the Danube, stands before book three.
Either way, at least some of this notebook was written in a camp, at war. Fourth, what that changes. Read book one again with a tent around it.
A tired man at the frontier, far from his family, sat down and listed, one by one, the people who had made him who he was. A great-grandfather. A tutor.

teach.h: A GRATITUDE LIST, IN A TENT.

teach.b: And when book two begins tomorrow, the camp is still there.

how: Some people who keep a journal in Marcus's spirit write wherever they happen to be, on commutes, breaks or travels, rather than waiting for a quiet desk.

games.q: you're the emperor at a frontier camp, after a long day of war business. it's cold, and you're tired. what do you do?
o: sleep; there's nothing left to give.
write notes to yourself in Greek, about how to live.
dictate a triumphant report for Rome.
games.why: the notes in the manuscripts suggest at least some of the Meditations was written in camps like this.

practice: Picture the camp: a cold river, tents, smoke, soldiers' voices outside, and inside one tent a man writing to himself.
Now picture the least likely place you might write something, a bus seat, a hospital waiting room, your car in a parking lot, and imagine one true line you'd write there, just for you.

wordCard.voice: Quadi. The Germanic people on the Danube frontier, near whose river Marcus's notebook was written, in camp, during war. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: written in camp. A gratitude list, in the middle of a war. Day five hundred thirty, done.
